segments.title: Why journalists can use anonymous sources but historians cannot
segments.summary: Journalists can vet protected sources while reporting urgent events, whereas historians must leave an evidence trail that another scholar can inspect and test.
segments.body: Journalists often cover events while they are unfolding, when the public needs information and an informed source may speak only if protected from professional or personal consequences. The reporter can meet that person, ask questions, compare claims, and decide whether the source is trustworthy even when the public cannot see the source's identity. A joke about ancient Greek predecessors receiving information in dreams introduces the modern historian's stricter obligation. The argument must rest on a chain of sources that another scholar can follow and use to test its factual basis. An anonymous source whose identity and context cannot be recovered breaks that reproducible chain. Both professions require verification. Journalists make a real-time trust decision, while historians must leave sources that later researchers can follow.
segments.question: Why can journalists use anonymous sources when historians generally cannot?
segments.answerShort: A journalist can personally assess a protected source while reporting a current event, but a historian must provide an evidence trail that later researchers can independently check.

evidence.note: Dr Clarke explains why immediate reporting may depend on protected sources whom a journalist can assess directly.
He contrasts that practice with the historian's duty to provide a source trail another scholar can follow and substantiate.

segments.title: Anonymous newspaper sources turn historians into detectives
segments.summary: Anonymous attribution in contemporary newspapers can force historians to reconstruct who supplied a claim before treating the report as dependable evidence.
segments.body: A newspaper article from the period does not automatically solve the historian's source problem if its decisive information came from an unnamed person. Without knowing who spoke, the researcher cannot readily substantiate the report or decide whether its information deserves trust. The historian may therefore have to reconstruct who could have leaked the information and which journalist or paper received it. Work with early twentieth-century newspapers, especially papers from the 1920s and 1930s, becomes a form of historical detective work because writers often try to disguise an otherwise obvious source. That reconstruction complicates research, but it also makes the resulting analysis easier for other historians to substantiate.

evidence.note: He explains why anonymously sourced contemporary journalism remains difficult for historians to trust.
He describes the benefits of substantiation and the detective work required by newspapers from the early twentieth century through the 1930s.
The conclusion ties this evidentiary problem to historians' different treatment of sources.
